family-afro-asiatic.name: Afro-Asiatic Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most Afro-Asiatic languages have a masculine/feminine gender distinction that triggers agreement on verbs, adjectives, pronouns, and (in Semitic) numerals. Some Cushitic and Omotic languages have more complex gender/class systems. Gender assignment is partly semantic, partly arbitrary.

linguisticChallenges.rootBasedMorphology: Semitic branch languages use a root-and-pattern (templatic) morphological system where consonantal roots (typically 3 consonants) are combined with vowel patterns and affixes to derive meaning. This is fundamentally different from concatenative morphology and requires understanding of abstract root extraction. Other branches (Berber, Cushitic, Chadic) show varying degrees of this system.
linguisticChallenges.morphologicalComplexity: Afro-Asiatic languages span a wide range of morphological complexity — from extensive templatic morphology (Arabic, Hebrew) to more analytic structures (some Chadic languages). Verbal morphology is generally rich, encoding subject, sometimes object, tense, aspect, and mood.
linguisticChallenges.genderAgreement: The masculine/feminine gender system triggers agreement chains across clauses. Number and gender interact in complex ways — e.g., Arabic numerals show reverse gender agreement (feminine numeral with masculine noun and vice versa).
linguisticChallenges.pluralFormation: Plural formation is highly irregular across the family. Semitic languages famously use 'broken plurals' (internal vowel changes) alongside 'sound plurals' (suffixation), with no reliable rule for predicting which pattern a noun takes.
linguisticChallenges.wordOrderVariation: Word order varies significantly: VSO (Classical Arabic, Hebrew), SVO (many modern varieties), SOV (some Cushitic, Omotic). Genus-level cards specify word order for each branch.

family-afro-asiatic.notes: Family card for Afro-Asiatic (~380 members). Covers Semitic (Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic), Berber, Cushitic (Somali, Oromo), Chadic (Hausa), Omotic, and Egyptian. The genus-semitic.json card provides Semitic-specific properties. Script and direction are null because the family includes both RTL (Arabic, Hebrew) and LTR (Amharic/Ge'ez, Latin for Hausa/Berber) scripts.

family-algic.name: Algic Family

formality.description: Algic languages express formality through kinship-based respectful address, ceremonial discourse patterns, and elder-directed speech. There is no European-style T-V pronominal distinction. Respectful language is context-dependent rather than pronoun-driven.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Algic languages use an animacy distinction (animate vs. inanimate noun classes) rather than masculine/feminine grammatical gender. Verbs, demonstratives, quantifiers, and plural markers all agree with the animacy class of their head noun. Animacy assignment is partially arbitrary — some inanimate objects are grammatically animate.

linguisticChallenges.polysynthesis: Algic languages are highly polysynthetic. Verbs carry person markers for both subject and object, plus tense, aspect, mode, and derivational morphemes. A single verb form can express what requires a full clause in English. Word-level MT is fundamentally inadequate for these languages.
linguisticChallenges.animacySystem: The animate/inanimate noun classification triggers agreement throughout the sentence — verbs, demonstratives, and quantifiers all agree with noun animacy. This binary classification system has no parallel in most target languages. Animacy assignment must be memorized per noun.
linguisticChallenges.directInverseVoice: Algic languages use a direct/inverse voice system that marks whether the agent or patient is higher on a person/animacy hierarchy, replacing the active/passive distinction found in European languages. Direct forms are used when the agent outranks the patient; inverse forms when the patient outranks the agent.
linguisticChallenges.obviation: Algic languages have a proximate/obviative distinction for third-person referents — when two third-person entities interact, one is marked as 'proximate' (topical) and the other as 'obviative' (secondary). This discourse-tracking system is typologically rare and routinely mishandled by MT.
linguisticChallenges.headMarking: Algic languages are predominantly head-marking — grammatical relations are marked on the head of a phrase (the verb) rather than on dependents (nouns). This is the opposite of dependent-marking languages like Latin or Turkish.

family-algic.notes: Family card for Algic (~50 members). This is the broader family containing Algonquian (Cree, Ojibwe, Blackfoot, Mi'kmaq, etc.) plus Yurok and Wiyot. The existing family-algonquian.json card covers the Algonquian branch specifically. This card replaces a previous family-algonquian.json concept at the top-level family position — Algic is the correct top-level family node.

regions.region: Canada (coast to coast), United States (Great Lakes, Plains, Northeast, Southeast)

family-algonquian.name: Algonquian Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Languages in this family utilize an animacy distinction (animate vs inanimate noun classes) rather than grammatical gender. Verbs, demonstratives, and quantifiers agree with the animacy class of their head noun. Animacy classification is partially arbitrary — some objects (e.g., raspberries, pants) are grammatically animate.

formality.description: Algonquian languages express formality through kinship-based respectful address and ceremonial language rather than pronominal T-V systems. Elder address and ceremonial contexts use specific vocabulary and discourse patterns.

linguisticChallenges.polysynthesis: Algonquian languages are highly polysynthetic. Verbs carry person markers for both subject and object, plus tense, aspect, mode, and derivational morphemes. A single verb form can express what requires a full clause in English.
linguisticChallenges.animacySystem: The animate/inanimate noun classification triggers agreement throughout the sentence — verbs, demonstratives, and quantifiers all agree with noun animacy. This system has no parallel in European languages.
linguisticChallenges.obviation: Algonquian languages have a proximate/obviative distinction for third-person referents — when two third-person entities interact, one is marked as 'proximate' (topical) and the other as 'obviative' (non-topical). This discourse-tracking system is typologically rare.
linguisticChallenges.directInverse: The direct/inverse voice system marks whether the subject or object is higher on the person/animacy hierarchy, replacing the active/passive distinction found in European languages.

contactInfluences.notes: English-only schooling policies (residential/boarding schools) severely disrupted intergenerational transmission across all Algonquian languages.
Fur trade era borrowings and missionary contact. French influence strongest in eastern Algonquian languages (Cree, Algonquin, Ojibwe).

family-algonquian.notes: Family template for Algonquian languages (Cree, Ojibwe, Blackfoot, Mi'kmaq, etc.). All share polysynthetic morphology, animacy-based noun classification, obviation, and the direct/inverse voice system.

family-atlantic-congo.name: Atlantic-Congo Family

formality.description: Atlantic-Congo languages generally lack European-style T-V pronominal distinctions. Formality is expressed through kinship-based address, honorific vocabulary, greetings protocols, and discourse style. Many languages have elaborate greeting systems that encode social hierarchy.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Atlantic-Congo languages overwhelmingly use noun class systems (5–20+ classes) rather than masculine/feminine grammatical gender. Noun classes categorize by semantic properties (human, animal, plant, abstract, mass, diminutive, augmentative, etc.) and trigger agreement on verbs, adjectives, pronouns, and demonstratives. These are NOT equivalent to European grammatical gender.

linguisticChallenges.nounClassSystems: The vast majority of Atlantic-Congo languages have noun class systems with 5–20+ classes. Agreement marking cascades through entire clauses — verbs, adjectives, possessives, demonstratives, and relative markers must all agree with the noun class of their head noun. This cascading agreement is a major challenge for MT systems trained primarily on European languages.
linguisticChallenges.toneSystem: Most Atlantic-Congo languages are tonal, using pitch to distinguish both lexical items and grammatical categories (tense, aspect, mood). Tone is rarely marked in standard orthography, creating systematic ambiguity. Many have tone sandhi (contextual tone changes) that further complicates analysis.
linguisticChallenges.agglutination: Most members are agglutinative, particularly in verbal morphology. Verbs carry subject markers, object markers, tense/aspect/mood, negation, and derivational morphemes as affixes. A single verb form can encode a complete predication.
linguisticChallenges.serialVerbConstructions: Serial verb constructions (SVCs) are widespread — sequences of verbs sharing arguments without overt coordination or subordination. These have no structural equivalent in most target languages and require careful paraphrasing.
linguisticChallenges.ideophones: Atlantic-Congo languages make extensive use of ideophones — expressive words that evoke sensory imagery (sound, shape, texture, motion, color). These are often untranslatable and require creative adaptation.

family-atlantic-congo.notes: Family card for the Atlantic-Congo family (~1,367 members), the world's largest language family by member count. Includes Bantu, Kwa, Gur, Adamawa, Atlantic, and many other branches. All share noun class systems and predominantly agglutinative verbal morphology. The genus-bantu.json card extends this for the Bantu subgroup specifically.

regions.region: West, Central, East, and Southern Africa

family-austroasiatic.name: Austroasiatic Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Austroasiatic languages lack grammatical gender. Some have classifier systems that categorize nouns by semantic properties, but these are not gender systems.

linguisticChallenges.registerSystems: Mon-Khmer languages frequently have phonation register systems — breathy vs. clear voice, or tense vs. lax register — that distinguish lexical items. These interact with vowel quality and tone in complex ways that are poorly represented in standard orthography.
linguisticChallenges.sesquisyllabicPhonology: Many Austroasiatic languages exhibit sesquisyllabic word structure — words consist of a main stressed syllable preceded by a reduced presyllable (a 'minor syllable'). This phonological pattern affects morphological analysis and word boundary detection.
linguisticChallenges.richVowelSystems: Austroasiatic languages are famous for exceptionally large vowel inventories. Some Mon-Khmer languages have 20+ distinct vowels. Romanized transcriptions often use unfamiliar diacritics or digraphs that MT systems may corrupt.
linguisticChallenges.infixingMorphology: Unlike most language families, Austroasiatic languages make productive use of infixes — morphemes inserted into the middle of a root. This prefixing and infixing morphology differs from the suffixation-dominant patterns familiar to most MT systems.
linguisticChallenges.morphologicalDiversity: The family spans from highly analytic/isolating (Vietnamese, Khmer) to agglutinative (Munda languages of India). This range is comparable to Indo-European's morphological diversity.
linguisticChallenges.toneVsRegister: Some members (like Vietnamese) have developed full tone systems, while others use voice register contrasts. In some languages, historical registers have split into tonal distinctions. This creates inconsistency in how phonological contrasts are orthographically marked.

family-austroasiatic.notes: Family card for Austroasiatic (~159 members). Covers Mon-Khmer branch (Vietnamese, Khmer, Mon) and Munda branch (Santali, Mundari). Properties vary significantly between branches — Mon-Khmer is mostly analytic/SVO while Munda is agglutinative/SOV. Script is null because members use Latin (Vietnamese), Khmer, Thai-derived, and Indic scripts.

regions.region: Vietnam, Cambodia, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Malaysia, India (Jharkhand/Odisha)

family-dravidian.name: Dravidian Family

formality.description: Dravidian languages have elaborate honorific/formality systems encoded in pronouns, verb conjugation, and vocabulary. Most distinguish at least three levels: intimate, neutral, and respectful/honorific. Tamil and Kannada have particularly complex systems where verb endings change based on the social register.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Gender systems vary within Dravidian. Tamil and Malayalam distinguish rational (human) vs. irrational (non-human) rather than masculine/feminine. Telugu and Kannada have masculine/feminine/neuter systems. In most Dravidian languages, the gender distinction is primarily reflected in third-person pronouns and verb agreement, not on nouns themselves.

linguisticChallenges.agglutinativeMorphology: Dravidian languages are highly agglutinative — suffixes are chained onto roots to encode case, number, tense, aspect, mood, negation, and more. A single verb form can carry 5–8 suffixes. Tamil verbal morphology alone has over 200 distinct finite forms per verb. MT must handle these affix chains without corrupting morpheme boundaries.
linguisticChallenges.relativeParticiples: Dravidian languages use relative participles (verbal adjectives) instead of relative clauses with pronouns. The equivalent of 'the man who came' is constructed as '[came] man' using a participial form. This is a fundamental structural difference from English that MT commonly mishandles.
linguisticChallenges.retroflexConsonants: All Dravidian languages distinguish retroflex consonants (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ḷ, ṛ) from dental consonants. These distinctions are phonemic and must be preserved in romanized output. Conflating retroflex and dental consonants changes word meaning.
linguisticChallenges.clusivityDistinctions: Some Dravidian languages (Tamil, Malayalam) distinguish inclusive 'we' (including addressee) from exclusive 'we' (excluding addressee). English 'we' is ambiguous and must be carefully resolved based on context.
linguisticChallenges.complexPostpositionalSystem: Dravidian languages are strictly postpositional (no prepositions). Spatial and temporal relations are expressed through case suffixes and postpositions. English prepositional phrases must be restructured as postpositional constructions.
linguisticChallenges.echoWords: Dravidian languages productively form echo words (e.g., Tamil: kaapi-giippi 'coffee and the like') to express generalization. These have no direct English equivalent and are easily broken by MT.

family-dravidian.notes: Family card for Dravidian (~85 members). Covers South Dravidian (Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada), South-Central (Telugu), Central (Kolami, Parji), and North (Brahui, Kurukh). Script is null because major members use Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and other scripts. Gender is marked true but the systems vary — see inclusiveGuidance.

regions.region: South India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana), also Pakistan (Brahui)

family-eskimo-aleut.name: Eskimo-Aleut Family

formality.description: Eskimo-Aleut languages express formality through kinship-based address and discourse style rather than pronominal T-V distinctions. Respectful language for elders and ceremonial contexts uses specific discourse markers, vocabulary, and indirect speech patterns.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Eskimo-Aleut languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns do not distinguish gender. Third-person referents are tracked through demonstrative systems and switch-reference rather than gendered pronouns.

linguisticChallenges.extremePolysynthesis: Eskimo-Aleut languages are among the most polysynthetic languages in the world — a single word can encode what would be an entire sentence in English. Verbs carry subject, object, tense, aspect, mood, and multiple derivational morphemes. Inuktitut tusaatsiarunnanngittualuujunga ('I can't hear very well') is a single word. Word-level and even phrase-level MT is fundamentally inadequate.
linguisticChallenges.ergativity: Most Eskimo-Aleut languages use ergative-absolutive case alignment — the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently from both the subject of an intransitive verb and the object. This is the opposite of nominative-accusative systems (English, most European languages) and requires a fundamentally different approach to argument mapping.
linguisticChallenges.incorporatedMorphology: Noun incorporation is highly productive — nouns can be incorporated into verb stems to create complex predicates. This creates 'words' with no single-word equivalent in target languages. The incorporated noun is not a separate syntactic entity.
linguisticChallenges.dualNumber: Eskimo-Aleut languages distinguish singular, dual, and plural number — there are separate forms for 'two of something'. This three-way number distinction must be properly handled; most target languages only have singular/plural.
linguisticChallenges.demonstrativeSystems: Elaborate demonstrative systems distinguish referents by distance, visibility, position relative to speaker, and motion. Inuktitut has 30+ demonstrative roots. These fine-grained spatial distinctions have no equivalent in most target languages.
linguisticChallenges.dialectalVariation: Significant dialectal variation across communities, even within the same language. Written standardization is often contested or incomplete. Different communities may use Latin script, Canadian Syllabics (ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑐᑦ), or Cyrillic.

family-eskimo-aleut.notes: Family card for Eskimo-Aleut (~14 members). Covers Inuit (Inuktitut, Inuinnaqtun, Kalaallisut, Iñupiaq), Yupik (Central Alaskan Yup'ik, Siberian Yupik), and Aleut. Promoted from genus-level to family-level card. Script is null because members use Latin, Canadian Syllabics (Unified Canadian Aboriginal Syllabics), and historically Cyrillic.

regions.region: Canada (Nunavut, NWT, northern Quebec/Nunavik, Labrador), USA (Alaska), Greenland, Russia (Chukotka)

family-indo-european.name: Indo-European Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most Indo-European languages have grammatical gender (2–3 genders: masculine/feminine, or masculine/feminine/neuter). Some branches (e.g., modern English, Bengali, Persian) have lost grammatical gender. Gender triggers agreement on articles, adjectives, pronouns, and sometimes verbs. Genus-level cards specify exact gender systems for each branch.

linguisticChallenges.inflectionalMorphology: Indo-European languages are predominantly inflectional (fusional) — a single morpheme can encode multiple grammatical categories simultaneously (e.g., case + number + gender in a single suffix). The degree of inflection varies enormously, from minimal (English, Persian) to extensive (Sanskrit, Lithuanian, Russian).
linguisticChallenges.agreementSystems: Most members have agreement systems where adjectives, determiners, and/or verbs must agree with nouns in gender, number, and/or case. Failure to maintain agreement is a common MT error.
linguisticChallenges.diverseWordOrders: Word order varies significantly across branches: SVO (Romance, Germanic, Slavic), SOV (Indic, Iranian), VSO (Celtic, some archaic stages). Some branches have relatively free word order with pragmatic reordering (Slavic, Baltic).
linguisticChallenges.scriptDiversity: The family uses Latin, Cyrillic, Devanagari, Arabic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek, Bengali, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, and other scripts. Script-specific handling is critical — genus cards specify script requirements.

family-indo-european.notes: Family card for Indo-European (~648 members). This is deliberately broad — most specific translation-relevant properties are defined at the genus level (genus-romance.json, genus-slavic.json, genus-germanic.json, genus-indic.json, genus-iranian.json, genus-celtic.json, etc.). Properties set to null here vary too much within the family to generalize.

regions.region: Europe, South Asia, Central Asia, Americas, Oceania

family-otomanguean.name: Otomanguean Family

linguisticChallenges.tonalComplexity: Otomanguean languages are tonal, many with complex tonal systems (Mixtec varieties have up to 8+ tone levels/contours). Tone often carries both lexical and grammatical information. Orthographic representation of tone varies across communities and is often incomplete.
linguisticChallenges.headInitial: Most Otomanguean languages are head-initial (VSO or VOS word order), which differs from the SOV or SVO patterns more familiar to MT systems.

family-otomanguean.notes: Minimal family card for Otomanguean (~180 members). A major Mesoamerican language family including Zapotec, Mixtec, Otomi, Mazatec, Chinantec, and others. All spoken in Mexico. Tonal systems and head-initial word order are the most consistently shared features. Many members are endangered.

regions.region: Oaxaca, Puebla, Guerrero, State of Mexico, Hidalgo, and surrounding states

family-pama-nyungan.name: Pama-Nyungan Family

linguisticChallenges.freeWordOrder: Pama-Nyungan languages are famous for relatively free word order — grammatical relations are encoded by case suffixes rather than position. Pragmatic factors (topic, focus, emphasis) determine word order.
linguisticChallenges.ergativity: Most members use ergative-absolutive case alignment — the subject of a transitive verb takes a special ergative case marker, while both intransitive subjects and transitive objects are unmarked (absolutive). Some show split ergativity conditioned by tense or NP type.

family-pama-nyungan.notes: Minimal family card for Pama-Nyungan (~261 members). The largest family of Australian Aboriginal languages, covering most of the Australian continent. Free word order and ergative alignment are the most consistently shared typological features. Many members are critically endangered or extinct.

regions.region: Most of the Australian continent (all except parts of northern Australia)

family-sino-tibetan.name: Sino-Tibetan Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Sino-Tibetan languages overwhelmingly lack grammatical gender. Pronouns are typically gender-neutral in spoken forms (though some writing systems, like Chinese, have introduced gendered third-person pronouns under Western influence).

linguisticChallenges.tonalSystems: The vast majority of Sino-Tibetan languages are tonal, using pitch contours to distinguish lexical meaning. Tone systems range from 2 tones (some Tibeto-Burman) to 9+ (Cantonese). Tonal accuracy is critical — wrong tone = wrong word. MT systems frequently produce tone errors when generating romanized output.
linguisticChallenges.classifierSystems: Classifier (measure word) systems are pervasive across the family. Nouns require specific classifiers when counted or quantified, and classifier selection depends on semantic properties of the noun (shape, size, animacy, etc.). Using the wrong classifier sounds unnatural or comical.
linguisticChallenges.topicProminence: Most Sino-Tibetan languages are topic-prominent rather than subject-prominent. The topic-comment structure differs fundamentally from English SVO patterns and cannot be handled by simple word reordering.
linguisticChallenges.proDrop: Subject and object pronouns are routinely dropped when recoverable from context. MT systems trained on English tend to over-generate pronouns in Sino-Tibetan output.
linguisticChallenges.morphologicalDiversity: The family spans a huge morphological range: Sinitic languages are analytic/isolating (few affixes), while Tibeto-Burman languages range from analytic to highly agglutinative. Genus cards specify morphological type.
linguisticChallenges.scriptDiversity: The family uses CJK characters, Tibetan script, Burmese script, various Indic-derived scripts, and Latin (for romanization and some minority languages). Script handling differs radically between branches.

family-sino-tibetan.notes: Family card for Sino-Tibetan (~452 members). Covers Sinitic (Chinese varieties), Tibeto-Burman, and other branches. Properties vary enormously between Sinitic (analytic, CJK) and Tibeto-Burman (agglutinative, various scripts). Genus-level cards (genus-sinitic.json etc.) provide branch-specific properties.

regions.region: China, Tibet, Myanmar, Nepal, Bhutan, NE India, mainland Southeast Asia

family-tai-kadai.name: Tai-Kadai Family

formality.description: Tai-Kadai languages generally express formality through particles, pronouns of politeness, and register-specific vocabulary rather than inflectional changes. Thai and Lao have elaborate pronoun systems encoding social hierarchy, gender of speaker, and formality level.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Tai-Kadai languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns are generally gender-neutral, though some languages (e.g., Thai) have gendered politeness particles (ครับ/khrap for male speakers, ค่ะ/kha for female speakers) that are pragmatic rather than grammatical.

linguisticChallenges.tonalAccuracy: All major Tai-Kadai languages are tonal (typically 4–8 tones). Tone is lexically contrastive — the same syllable with different tones has completely different meanings. Romanized transcriptions require accurate tone diacritics. MT systems frequently produce tone errors.
linguisticChallenges.classifierSelection: Extensive classifier (measure word/numeral classifier) systems are universal in the family. Every noun has one or more associated classifiers used in counting, quantification, and reference. Using the wrong classifier is a clear non-native error.
linguisticChallenges.serialVerbConstructions: Serial verb constructions are the primary means of expressing complex events — multiple verbs are strung together without conjunctions or subordination. These sequences have specific ordering constraints and cannot be decomposed into separate clauses without losing meaning.
linguisticChallenges.noInflection: Tai-Kadai languages have virtually no inflectional morphology — no conjugation, declension, or agreement. Tense, aspect, and mood are expressed through particles and word order. MT systems may incorrectly generate inflected forms.
linguisticChallenges.wordBoundaries: Thai and Lao scripts do not use spaces between words, only between clauses or sentences. Word segmentation is a critical preprocessing challenge for MT. Even with Latin-script languages, compound words and collocations create boundary ambiguity.
linguisticChallenges.topicComment: Topic-comment structures are common, where the topic of a sentence is fronted regardless of its grammatical role. This pragmatic word order cannot be handled by rigid syntactic transformations.

family-tai-kadai.notes: Family card for Tai-Kadai (~88 members). Covers Tai branch (Thai, Lao, Shan, Zhuang), Kam-Sui, Hlai, and other branches. Script is null because members use Thai, Lao, Tai Tham, New Tai Lue, Zhuang Latin, and other scripts.

regions.region: Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, Myanmar, southern China (Guangxi, Yunnan, Guizhou)

family-trans-new-guinea.name: Trans-New Guinea Family

linguisticChallenges.medialVerbs: Trans-New Guinea languages widely use medial verb forms in clause chains — sequences of dependent clauses marked for same-subject or different-subject relative to the following clause. This switch-reference system has no parallel in most target languages.
linguisticChallenges.agglutination: Most members are agglutinative with SOV word order. Verb-final structure is consistent across the family.

family-trans-new-guinea.notes: Minimal family card for Trans-New Guinea (~312 members). One of the largest language families but with limited shared properties documented for translation purposes. Members are spread across the highlands of New Guinea. SOV word order and medial verb/switch-reference systems are the most consistently shared features.

regions.country: Papua New Guinea and Indonesian Papua
regions.region: New Guinea highlands and surrounding areas

family-turkic.name: Turkic Family

formality.description: Most Turkic languages have a T-V pronominal distinction: informal singular (sen/sin) vs. formal/plural (siz/siz). Formality is also expressed through verb endings that agree with the chosen pronoun. Some languages (Uzbek, Kazakh) distinguish additional levels of deference.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Turkic languages have no grammatical gender whatsoever — no gendered pronouns, no gendered agreement, no gendered nouns. The third-person pronoun (o/ol/u) is gender-neutral. When translating from gendered source languages, gender information is simply lost unless explicitly stated.

linguisticChallenges.vowelHarmony: All Turkic languages have vowel harmony — suffixes change their vowels to harmonize with the root vowel (front/back, rounded/unrounded). Suffix forms are predictable but MT systems frequently generate disharmonic forms. Each language has its own harmony rules and exceptions.
linguisticChallenges.extensiveAgglutination: Turkic languages are highly agglutinative — verbs and nouns can carry long chains of suffixes encoding tense, aspect, mood, person, number, negation, causative, passive, reciprocal, and more. A single Turkish word like 'Avrupalılaştıramadıklarımızdanmışsınızcasına' is grammatically valid.
linguisticChallenges.definitenessWithoutArticles: Turkic languages lack definite/indefinite articles. Definiteness is conveyed through word order (definite objects precede the verb), accusative case marking (definite direct objects take accusative), and context. Translating English 'a' vs. 'the' requires structural decisions, not simple word substitution.
linguisticChallenges.relativeClauses: Turkic languages form relative clauses using participles placed before the noun, similar to Dravidian. The equivalent of 'the book that I read' is '[my reading] book'. This prenominal participial strategy differs fundamentally from English postnominal relative clauses.
linguisticChallenges.caseSystem: Most Turkic languages have 6–7 cases (nominative, accusative, dative, locative, ablative, genitive, and sometimes instrumental). Case suffixes interact with vowel harmony and consonant alternation rules.
linguisticChallenges.wordOrderFlexibility: While basic word order is SOV, word order is pragmatically flexible. Focused or emphasized elements move to immediately pre-verbal position. Topic elements can be fronted. This pragmatic reordering is not random — it encodes information structure.

family-turkic.notes: Family card for Turkic (~52 members). Covers Oghuz (Turkish, Azerbaijani, Turkmen), Kipchak (Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar), Karluk (Uzbek, Uyghur), Siberian (Sakha/Yakut, Tuvan), and others. Script is null because members use Latin (Turkish, Azerbaijani), Cyrillic (Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar), and Arabic (Uyghur, Ottoman) scripts. Most languages are shifting toward Latin.

regions.region: Turkey, Central Asia (Kazakhstan–Turkmenistan), Azerbaijan, Siberia, Xinjiang

family-uralic.name: Uralic Family

formality.description: Most major Uralic languages have T-V pronominal distinctions: Finnish sinä/te, Hungarian te/ön (or maga), Estonian sina/teie. The degree of formality encoding varies — Hungarian also has a definite/indefinite verb conjugation distinction that interacts with object reference.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Uralic languages overwhelmingly lack grammatical gender. Third-person pronouns are gender-neutral (Finnish hän, Hungarian ő, Estonian tema). When translating from gendered source languages, gender must be expressed lexically or left unspecified.

linguisticChallenges.extensiveCaseSystems: Uralic languages are famous for their extensive case systems — Finnish has 15 cases, Hungarian 18, Estonian 14. Each case has specific semantic and syntactic functions. MT systems trained primarily on languages with few cases (English, French) consistently produce case errors.
linguisticChallenges.agglutinativeMorphology: Uralic languages are agglutinative, building complex word forms by chaining suffixes. A single Finnish word form can encode case, number, possessive suffix, and clitic particles. Hungarian verbal morphology distinguishes definite and indefinite conjugations.
linguisticChallenges.possessiveSuffixes: Most Uralic languages express possession through suffixes on the possessed noun rather than separate possessive pronouns. Finnish talo-ni 'my house', talo-si 'your house'. This is a fundamental structural difference from most European languages.
linguisticChallenges.vowelHarmony: Finnish, Hungarian, and several other Uralic languages have vowel harmony systems where suffix vowels must harmonize with root vowels (front/back, and sometimes rounded/unrounded). Rules and exceptions differ by language.
linguisticChallenges.definitenessExpression: Most Uralic languages lack definite articles (Hungarian is a notable exception with a/az). Definiteness is expressed through word order, case marking, or context. Hungarian uniquely has a definite verb conjugation that marks object definiteness on the verb.
linguisticChallenges.negationVerb: Several Uralic languages (Finnish, Estonian, Sami) conjugate the negative auxiliary rather than the main verb — e.g., Finnish en puhu, et puhu, ei puhu ('I/you/s/he don't speak'). This is typologically unusual and MT systems often mishandle it.

family-uralic.notes: Family card for Uralic (~48 members). Covers Finnic (Finnish, Estonian, Karelian), Ugric (Hungarian, Mansi, Khanty), Sami, Samoyedic (Nenets, Selkup), and others. Script is Latin for the vast majority — only some historical/minority members use Cyrillic alongside Latin.

regions.region: Finland, Estonia, Hungary, northern Scandinavia (Sami), Russia (Komi, Udmurt, Mari, Mordvin, Nenets)

genus-bantu.name: Bantu Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Bantu languages express formality through pronoun choice, honorific vocabulary, and discourse style rather than strict T-V pronominal systems. Many use plural forms for singular formal address.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Bantu languages use noun class systems (not gender). Nouns are classified into classes (typically 10-18) affecting agreement on verbs, adjectives, and pronouns. These are NOT gendered — they categorize by semantic properties (human, animal, abstract, etc.).

linguisticChallenges.nounClassSystem: Bantu languages have extensive noun class systems (10-18 classes) that trigger agreement chains across entire sentences. Verbs, adjectives, possessives, and demonstratives must all agree with the noun class of their head noun. This cascading agreement is extremely difficult for MT.
linguisticChallenges.agglutination: Bantu languages are highly agglutinative — verbs can carry subject markers, object markers, tense, aspect, mood, negation, and derivational morphemes as prefixes and suffixes. A single verb form can encode a complete sentence.
linguisticChallenges.toneSystem: Most Bantu languages are tonal (high/low tone, sometimes contrastive). Tone distinguishes lexical items and grammatical categories but is rarely written in standard orthography, creating systematic ambiguity for MT.
linguisticChallenges.conjunctDisjunctMorphology: Many Bantu languages distinguish conjunct (focused) and disjunct (non-focused) verb forms, a pragmatic distinction that affects verb morphology but has no parallel in most other language families.

contactInfluences.notes: British colonial influence across eastern and southern Africa.
Swahili coast trade influence. Particularly strong in Swahili vocabulary.

genus-bantu.notes: Genus template for Bantu languages (Swahili, Zulu, Xhosa, Shona, Kinyarwanda, Luganda, etc.). All share noun class systems, agglutinative morphology, and tonal features.

genus-celtic.name: Celtic Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Celtic languages generally use register-based formality rather than strict T-V pronominal systems. Welsh has ti/chi (informal/formal 'you'), Irish uses universal 'tú', and Scottish Gaelic uses 'thu/sibh'. Formality is primarily expressed through vocabulary choice and discourse markers rather than extensive verb conjugation.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Celtic languages have masculine/feminine grammatical gender affecting nouns, adjectives, and initial mutations. No neuter gender. Gender-inclusive language conventions are still developing in Celtic languages.

linguisticChallenges.initialMutations: All Celtic languages have systems of initial consonant mutations (lenition, nasalization, aspiration) triggered by grammatical context. A word's first consonant changes based on what precedes it. This is the #1 source of MT errors in Celtic languages.
linguisticChallenges.vsoWordOrder: Celtic languages are Verb-Subject-Object (VSO), one of the rarest word orders globally. Most MT models default to SVO assumptions, producing unnatural Celtic output.
linguisticChallenges.prepositionConjugation: Celtic languages conjugate prepositions — prepositions inflect for person and number (e.g., Irish: agam 'at-me', agat 'at-you', aige 'at-him'). This is typologically unusual and not handled by most MT architectures.

contactInfluences.notes: Progressive replacement of Celtic languages in public domains. All Celtic languages are in various stages of revitalization against English dominance.
Religious and scholarly borrowings from Latin via early Christianity.

genus-celtic.notes: Genus template for Insular Celtic languages (Goidelic: Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Manx; Brythonic: Welsh, Breton, Cornish). All share VSO word order, initial mutations, and preposition conjugation.

genus-cree.name: Cree-Montagnais-Naskapi Continuum

formality.description: Cree languages do not have a European-style T-V distinction. Formality is expressed through respectful particles, verb forms, and lexical choices. The register system is shared across the continuum but specific vocabulary and orthography differ by variety.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Cree languages use an animacy distinction (animate vs inanimate noun classes) rather than grammatical gender. Verb conjugation, demonstratives, and plural marking all depend on animacy class.

variables.guidance: Variables are marked with braces `{count}`. Since Cree relies heavily on affixation, suffixes must attach directly to placeholders. Use a hyphen to separate the variable from grammatical affixes (e.g., `{count}-ak` or `{count}-a` for plurals).

linguisticChallenges.polysynthesis: All Cree varieties are highly polysynthetic. A single verb can incorporate subject/object pronouns, instrumentals, locations, and actions. Translate phrases conceptually rather than word-for-word.
linguisticChallenges.animacy: Verb conjugation changes completely based on whether the subject/object nouns are animate or inanimate. Ensure grammatical agreement. Animacy class is not always intuitive — e.g., 'rock' (asiniy) is animate.
linguisticChallenges.obviation: Cree uses a proximate/obviative system to track third-person referents. In discourse with multiple third persons, one is proximate (main) and others are obviative (secondary). MT systems frequently mishandle this.
linguisticChallenges.neologisms: Avoid literal translations of modern software concepts. Maintain English loanwords for modern UI elements when no community-accepted term exists. Each variety may coin different neologisms.
linguisticChallenges.dialectContinuum: The Cree-Montagnais-Naskapi varieties form a dialect continuum. Adjacent varieties are mutually intelligible; distant ones are not. Do NOT mix vocabulary from different varieties.

contactInfluences.period: fur trade era and missionary contact (17th–19th century)
contactInfluences.notes: French missionaries developed early Cree writing systems. French loanwords in eastern varieties (Innu, Atikamekw) are more numerous than in western varieties.
English is the dominant language of administration across all Cree territories. Code-switching is pervasive in younger speakers.
Southwestern Cree varieties (Plains, Swampy) share significant vocabulary with Ojibwe. The languages are closely related within Algonquian.

genus-cree.notes: Genus card for the Cree-Montagnais-Naskapi continuum. Individual variety cards (crk, csw, cwd, crm, crl, crj, atj, moe, nsk) extend this card and override with variety-specific data. macrolanguage is intentionally null here: only crj/crk/crl/crm/csw/cwd are ISO 639-3 members of the 'cre' macrolanguage (see cre.json members[]), and atj/moe/nsk/crg must not inherit a membership ISO does not assert. Members carry their own explicit macrolanguage field.

genus-eskimo-aleut.name: Eskimo-Aleut Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Eskimo-Aleut languages express formality through kinship-based address and discourse style rather than pronominal T-V distinctions. Respectful language for elders and ceremonial contexts uses specific discourse markers and vocabulary.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Eskimo-Aleut languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns do not distinguish gender.

linguisticChallenges.polysynthesis: Eskimo-Aleut languages are extremely polysynthetic — a single word can encode what would be an entire sentence in English. Verbs carry subject, object, tense, aspect, mood, and multiple derivational morphemes. Word-level MT is fundamentally inadequate.
linguisticChallenges.ergativity: Most Eskimo-Aleut languages are ergative-absolutive in case alignment, meaning the subject of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb receive different case markings. This is the opposite of English/European patterns.
linguisticChallenges.incorporatedMorphology: Noun incorporation is productive — nouns can be incorporated into verb stems to create complex predicates. This creates 'words' that have no single-word equivalent in target languages.
linguisticChallenges.dialectalVariation: Significant dialectal variation across communities, even within the same language. Written standardization is often contested or incomplete.

contactInfluences.notes: Colonial and administrative dominance. English-only schooling policies severely impacted intergenerational transmission.
French administrative influence in northern Quebec (Nunavik) and some Labrador communities.

genus-eskimo-aleut.notes: Genus template for Eskimo-Aleut languages (Inuktitut, Inuinnaqtun, Kalaallisut, Yupik varieties, etc.). All share extreme polysynthesis, ergative alignment, and noun incorporation.

genus-germanic.name: Germanic Languages

formality.description: Most Germanic languages have T-V pronominal distinctions: German du/Sie, Dutch je(jij)/u, Swedish du/ni (historically, now largely replaced by du-reform), Norwegian du/De (archaic). English is the major exception, having lost its T-V distinction (thou/you → universal you). Icelandic also lacks a formal pronoun. Default to formal (V) in professional contexts for languages that retain it.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most Germanic languages have grammatical gender, but systems vary: German, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål have masculine/feminine/neuter. Dutch and Swedish have common/neuter (two genders). Danish has common/neuter. English has lost grammatical gender almost entirely (retained only in pronouns). Gender triggers agreement on articles, adjectives, and pronouns.

linguisticChallenges.compoundWordFormation: Germanic languages (especially German, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Icelandic) form compound nouns by concatenation without spaces: German Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaft. Compound splitting for translation and compound generation in the target are both error-prone. English uses spaces in compounds, while other Germanic languages do not.
linguisticChallenges.separablePrefixVerbs: German and Dutch have separable prefix verbs (German: anfangen → ich fange an; Dutch: opbellen → ik bel op) where the prefix detaches and moves to the end of the clause. This creates long-distance dependencies that MT systems must track across clause boundaries.
linguisticChallenges.v2WordOrder: Most Germanic languages (German, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish) follow V2 (verb-second) word order in main clauses — the finite verb must be the second constituent regardless of what fills first position. Subordinate clauses have verb-final order (German, Dutch). This systematic word order alternation is a consistent source of MT errors.
linguisticChallenges.articleSystem: Germanic languages have both definite and indefinite articles, but their realization varies: Scandinavian languages suffix the definite article (Swedish hus-et 'the house'), while German/Dutch/English use freestanding articles. The double definiteness of Scandinavian (both suffix and freestanding article with adjectives) is a further complexity.
linguisticChallenges.caseVestiges: Full case systems survive in German (4 cases) and Icelandic (4 cases). Other Germanic languages have reduced case to pronouns only (English I/me, Swedish jag/mig) or lost it almost entirely (Dutch, Danish). German case interacts with gender and number to create complex declension tables.
linguisticChallenges.modalParticles: German and Dutch make extensive use of modal particles (doch, mal, ja, schon, eben; toch, maar, wel, even) that add nuance, emphasis, or pragmatic force to sentences. These particles have no direct equivalents in most other languages and are frequently dropped or mistranslated by MT.

genus-germanic.notes: Genus card for Germanic languages (English, German, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Icelandic, Afrikaans, Yiddish, etc.). All use Latin script. T-V formality applies to most members but not English or Icelandic. Gender system varies from 3-gender (German) to 2-gender (Dutch, Swedish) to none (English).

regions.region: Britain, Germany, Netherlands, Scandinavia, Iceland, global (English diaspora), South Africa (Afrikaans)

genus-indic.name: Indic (Indo-Aryan) Languages

formality.description: Indic languages have elaborate multi-level honorific systems that go far beyond European T-V. Hindi-Urdu distinguishes three levels: tū (intimate), tum (familiar), āp (formal/respectful). Bengali has tui/tumi/āpni. Many have distinct verb conjugations for each level. Honorifics extend to vocabulary — different verbs for 'eat', 'come', 'go' depending on the social status of the referent. Default to the highest formal register for professional/UI contexts.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most Indic languages have a binary masculine/feminine gender system (Hindi, Punjabi, Marathi, Gujarati). Some have additionally neuter (Marathi). Bengali and Assamese have lost grammatical gender. Gender triggers agreement on verbs, adjectives, and postpositions. Assignment is partly semantic, partly morphological.

linguisticChallenges.complexVerbalSystem: Indic languages have elaborate compound verb constructions — light verbs (vector verbs) combine with main verbs to express completion, benefaction, malefaction, and speaker attitude. Hindi jā (go), le (take), de (give), ḍāl (throw) combine as completive/intensive markers: kar denā 'to do (for someone)', kha lenā 'to eat up'. These compound verbs have no compositional translation.
linguisticChallenges.conjunctVerbs: Many Indic languages form predicates by combining a noun/adjective with a light verb: Hindi madad karnā 'help do' = 'to help', safāī karnā 'cleaning do' = 'to clean'. These conjunct verb constructions are the primary predicate-forming strategy and cannot be translated word-by-word.
linguisticChallenges.postpositionalSystem: Indic languages are strictly SOV with postpositions (not prepositions). Nouns take case markers that are postpositions: Hindi ghar mẽ 'house in' = 'in the house'. English prepositional phrases must be completely restructured.
linguisticChallenges.honorificRegisters: Verb conjugation, pronoun choice, vocabulary, and even postpositions change based on the social relationship between speaker and referent. Using the wrong register is a serious social error — more than just a stylistic issue.
linguisticChallenges.echoWordFormation: Indic languages productively form echo words by replacing the initial consonant/vowel of a word to express generalization: Hindi chāy-vāy 'tea and such things', khānā-vānā 'food and stuff'. These have no English equivalent.
linguisticChallenges.retroflexConsonants: All Indic languages distinguish retroflex from dental consonants (ṭ/t, ḍ/d, ṇ/n). These are separate phonemes that must be preserved in romanized output. Conflating them changes word meaning.
linguisticChallenges.scriptDiversity: Major Indic languages use different scripts: Devanagari (Hindi, Marathi, Nepali), Bengali-Assamese, Gujarati, Gurmukhi (Punjabi), Odia, Sinhala. Each script requires specific rendering support. Nastaliq/Shahmukhi (Arabic-based) is used for Urdu and some Punjabi.

contactInfluences.period: parent language (Prakrit stage ~3rd century BCE onward)
contactInfluences.notes: Sanskrit is the classical ancestor of Indic languages via Prakrits. Sanskrit continues as a major source of formal and technical vocabulary (tatsama borrowings).

Persian was the court language of the Mughal Empire. Hindi-Urdu, Punjabi, Bengali, and other northern Indic languages have extensive Persian/Arabic vocabulary, especially in administrative, literary, and cultural domains.

genus-indic.notes: Genus card for Indic (Indo-Aryan) languages (Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, Punjabi, Marathi, Gujarati, Odia, Sinhala, Nepali, Assamese, etc.). Script is null due to extreme script diversity — each major language uses a different script. All share SOV order, postpositions, compound verb constructions, and multi-level honorific systems.

regions.region: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Maldives

genus-iranian.name: Iranian Languages

formality.description: Iranian languages typically have elaborate politeness systems. Persian (Farsi) has an extremely rich taarof system with multiple levels of formality affecting pronouns (to/shomā), verb conjugation, vocabulary (separate 'eat' verbs for formal/informal), and elaborate self-deprecating/other-elevating conventions. Kurdish and other Iranian languages have simpler but still significant T-V systems.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most modern Iranian languages have lost grammatical gender. Persian, Tajik, and Kurdish (Sorani) have no grammatical gender — third-person pronouns are gender-neutral (Persian u/ān). Kurdish (Kurmanji) is an exception that retains masculine/feminine gender. Some Pamir languages also retain gender. When translating from gendered source languages, gender is typically expressed lexically.

linguisticChallenges.ezafeConstruction: Iranian languages use the ezāfe (ezafe) construction to link nouns to their modifiers — a connecting particle (Persian -e/-ye, Kurdish -î/-y) between the head noun and its adjective, possessor, or complement. The chain can extend to multiple modifiers: ketāb-e bozorg-e sabz-e man 'my big green book'. This left-branching modifier structure is the reverse of English word order.
linguisticChallenges.lightVerbSystem: Persian and other Iranian languages form the vast majority of their predicates using light verb constructions — a noun, adjective, or preverb combined with a small set of light verbs (kardan 'do', shodan 'become', zadan 'hit', dādan 'give', etc.). There are hundreds of these combinations, and they cannot be predicted from their components: gush dādan 'ear give' = 'to listen'.
linguisticChallenges.complexPredicates: Beyond light verbs, Iranian languages use complex predicates with preverbs that modify verb meaning. The preverb system creates extensive polysemy and idiomatic expressions that require memorization rather than compositional analysis.
linguisticChallenges.splitErgativity: Some Iranian languages (Kurdish Kurmanji, Pashto, and some others) show split ergativity — ergative-absolutive alignment in past tenses but nominative-accusative in present tenses. This means the same verb has different argument-marking patterns in different tenses.
linguisticChallenges.scriptVariation: Iranian languages are split between Arabic-derived scripts (Persian, Pashto, Kurdish Sorani — written RTL) and Latin script (Kurdish Kurmanji, Tajik historically). Tajik uses Cyrillic. This script split within a single genus requires handling multiple directionalities.
linguisticChallenges.differentialObjectMarking: Persian uses the postposition -rā to mark specific/definite direct objects, while indefinite objects are unmarked. This differential object marking has no exact English equivalent — translating 'a book' vs. 'the book' requires choosing whether to use -rā.

genus-iranian.notes: Genus card for Iranian languages (Persian/Farsi, Dari, Tajik, Kurdish, Pashto, Balochi, Ossetian, etc.). Script is null because members use Arabic-derived scripts (RTL), Latin, and Cyrillic. Direction is null because of the RTL/LTR split. Gender is marked false since most major members have lost it (Kurmanji being a notable exception).

regions.region: Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Kurdistan (Iraq/Turkey/Syria), Pakistan (Pashto/Balochi), Caucasus (Ossetian)

genus-philippine.name: Philippine Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Philippine languages generally lack European-style T-V distinction. Respect is expressed through po/ho particles, pronoun choice (2nd person plural for singular formal), and vocabulary selection.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Philippine languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns (siya/niya) are gender-neutral. No special inclusive conventions needed.

linguisticChallenges.focusSystem: Philippine languages use a voice/focus system (also called 'trigger' or 'alignment') where verbal morphology marks the semantic role of the syntactically prominent argument. This is NOT like active/passive voice — it's a fundamentally different system that most MT models handle poorly.
linguisticChallenges.spanishSubstrate: Extensive Spanish loanwords integrated into core vocabulary (numbers, days, months, food, religion, government). Code-mixing with Spanish-derived terms is the norm, not an error.
linguisticChallenges.englishCodeswitching: Taglish/Bislish/etc. (mixing with English) is ubiquitous in modern spoken and written language. Pure monolingual text can sound overly formal or archaic.
linguisticChallenges.reduplication: Productive reduplication for plurality, diminution, intensity, and aspect. Both full and partial reduplication are morphologically significant.

contactInfluences.notes: 333 years of colonization. Thousands of fully nativized loanwords.
Co-official language. Taglish/Bislish code-switching is the default register in urban areas.
Shared Austronesian vocabulary. Trade pidgin influence in southern Philippines.

genus-philippine.notes: Genus template for Philippine Austronesian languages. All Philippine languages share the focus/trigger system, extensive Spanish/English contact influence, and Latin script.

genus-polynesian.name: Polynesian Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Polynesian languages express formality through vocabulary choice, discourse particles, and speech style rather than pronominal T-V systems. Many have distinct ceremonial/oratorial registers for formal occasions.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Polynesian languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns are gender-neutral.

linguisticChallenges.particleSystem: Polynesian languages rely heavily on particles (tense/aspect markers, case markers, prepositions) rather than inflectional morphology. Word boundaries and particle placement are critical for meaning but difficult for MT to learn from limited data.
linguisticChallenges.limitedConsonantInventory: Most Polynesian languages have very small consonant inventories (8-15 consonants) and strict CV syllable structure. This creates many near-homophones distinguished only by vowel length (macrons/glottal stops), making diacritical accuracy critical.
linguisticChallenges.diacriticalSensitivity: Macrons (ā, ē, ī, ō, ū) and glottal stops (ʻ) are phonemic — they distinguish words with completely different meanings. Most MT systems strip or ignore these diacritics, producing ambiguous or incorrect output.
linguisticChallenges.culturalEmbedding: Many words carry deep cultural/spiritual meaning that cannot be directly translated. Neologisms for modern concepts must be carefully coined to avoid cultural inappropriateness.

contactInfluences.notes: Colonial and post-colonial English dominance across Polynesia. All Polynesian languages are in various stages of revitalization.

genus-polynesian.notes: Genus template for Polynesian languages (Māori, Hawaiian, Samoan, Tongan, Tahitian, etc.). All share particle-heavy syntax, limited consonant inventories, and critical diacritical sensitivity.

genus-romance.name: Romance Languages

formality.description: All major Romance languages have a T-V pronominal distinction: French tu/vous, Spanish tú/usted (and vos in Rioplatense), Portuguese tu/você/o senhor, Italian tu/Lei, Romanian tu/dumneavoastră, Catalan tu/vostè. The formal pronoun varies in grammatical person (2nd plural in French, 3rd singular in Italian/Spanish). Translation must select the correct register — defaulting to formal (V) for UI/professional contexts.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: All Romance languages have a binary masculine/feminine gender system (Romanian also has neuter). Gender is assigned to all nouns and triggers agreement on articles, adjectives, past participles, and pronouns. When the gender of a referent is unknown, most Romance languages default to masculine, but inclusive language practices are evolving rapidly (e.g., Spanish -e endings, French écriture inclusive with ·).

linguisticChallenges.cliticPlacement: Romance languages make extensive use of clitic pronouns (me, te, le, lo, la, etc.) that attach to verbs in specific positions. Clitic placement rules differ by language — proclitic (before verb) in most finite forms, enclitic (after verb) in infinitives, imperatives, and gerunds. Clitic climbing, clustering, and doubling add further complexity. Wrong clitic placement is immediately noticeable.
linguisticChallenges.subjunctiveMood: All Romance languages retain a productive subjunctive mood triggered by specific matrix predicates (desire, doubt, emotion, necessity), conjunctions (aunque, pour que), and negation contexts. The choice of indicative vs. subjunctive carries semantic weight — using the wrong mood changes meaning or sounds ungrammatical.
linguisticChallenges.genderedAgreement: Adjectives, articles, past participles, and some pronouns must agree with their head noun in gender and number. Agreement chains can span long distances in complex sentences. MT commonly produces agreement mismatches, especially in relative clauses and coordinated structures.
linguisticChallenges.proDropBehavior: Romance languages are pro-drop (except French, which requires overt subject pronouns in most contexts). Subject pronouns are only used for emphasis or disambiguation. Over-generating subject pronouns sounds unnatural in Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian.
linguisticChallenges.serialObjectPronouns: Multiple object clitics can co-occur (e.g., Spanish se lo digo, French je le lui donne), with strict ordering rules that differ between languages. Clitic combinations sometimes trigger morphological changes (Spanish le + lo → se lo).
linguisticChallenges.copulaDistinctions: Spanish and Portuguese distinguish ser/estar (permanent/temporary), Catalan distinguishes ser/estar/fer, and Italian distinguishes essere/stare. English 'to be' must be split based on context — misselection is a hallmark of poor translation.

contactInfluences.notes: Vulgar Latin is the direct ancestor of all Romance languages. Classical Latin continues to influence formal and technical vocabulary.

genus-romance.notes: Genus card for Romance languages (French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Romanian, Catalan, Galician, Occitan, etc.). All descend from Vulgar Latin and share T-V formality, M/F gender, SVO word order, subjunctive mood, and clitic pronoun systems. Individual language cards override with language-specific rules.

regions.region: Southern/Western Europe, Latin America, parts of Africa and Southeast Asia

genus-semitic.name: Semitic Languages

formality.description: Most Semitic languages have formality distinctions in address. Arabic uses anta/antum (singular/plural 2nd person, with plural doubling as formal). Hebrew uses ata/atem similarly. Amharic and Tigrinya have elaborate politeness systems with multiple address levels. Formality also affects vocabulary and discourse style.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: All Semitic languages have a binary masculine/feminine gender system. Gender triggers agreement on verbs, adjectives, pronouns, demonstratives, and (in Arabic) numerals. Second-person pronouns and verb forms distinguish gender of the addressee. Some nouns have both masculine and feminine plurals with different meanings. Gender agreement is pervasive and non-negotiable.

linguisticChallenges.rootPatternMorphology: Semitic languages use a non-concatenative (root-and-pattern) morphological system where consonantal roots (typically 3 consonants, sometimes 4) are interleaved with vowel patterns and affixes to derive meaning. Arabic root k-t-b + patterns yields: kataba 'he wrote', kitāb 'book', kātib 'writer', maktaba 'library', maktūb 'written'. This templatic system has no parallel in most target languages and cannot be handled by simple stemming.
linguisticChallenges.brokenPlurals: Semitic languages (especially Arabic) extensively use 'broken plurals' — internal vowel changes that form plurals rather than suffixation. Arabic kitāb → kutub, rajul → rijāl, bayt → buyūt. There are dozens of broken plural patterns with no reliable prediction rule. This is one of the most error-prone areas for MT.
linguisticChallenges.constructState: Semitic languages use the construct state (Arabic iḍāfa, Hebrew smikhut) to express genitive/possessive relationships by directly juxtaposing nouns. The first noun takes a special shortened form. Construct state chains can extend multiple nouns deep and have specific definiteness rules.
linguisticChallenges.shortVowelOmission: Arabic and Hebrew standard orthography largely omits short vowels (written in consonantal abjad scripts). This creates massive ambiguity — the same consonantal skeleton can represent multiple words. MT systems must disambiguate from context. Fully vowelized text (with diacritics) is used only in religious texts, children's books, and dictionaries.
linguisticChallenges.diglossiaAndRegister: Arabic exhibits extreme diglossia — Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) differs dramatically from spoken dialects (Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Maghreb, etc.) in phonology, morphology, syntax, and vocabulary. Written Arabic is almost exclusively MSA, while spoken communication uses dialect. MT must handle both registers.
linguisticChallenges.verbInitialWordOrder: Classical and formal Semitic languages favor VSO word order (Arabic, Classical Hebrew), while modern colloquial varieties tend toward SVO. The verb-initial position interacts with subject agreement — VS order in Arabic triggers different agreement patterns than SV order.

genus-semitic.notes: Genus card for Semitic languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic, Tigrinya, Aramaic, Maltese, etc.). Script is null because members use Arabic script (RTL), Hebrew script (RTL), Ge'ez/Ethiopic script (LTR), and Latin (Maltese, LTR). Direction is null due to this RTL/LTR split. Plural categories include all six CLDR categories as Arabic uses all of them.

regions.country: Middle East and Horn of Africa
regions.region: Arab world (Middle East and North Africa), Israel, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Malta

genus-sinitic.name: Sinitic (Chinese) Languages

formality.description: Sinitic languages express formality through vocabulary choice, discourse style, and specific honorific/humble forms rather than pronominal T-V systems. Mandarin nǐ/nín (你/您) is a T-V distinction, but most other Sinitic varieties rely primarily on lexical register (formal vs. colloquial word choice, classical vs. vernacular vocabulary). Written Chinese formal register draws heavily on Classical Chinese (文言文) vocabulary.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Sinitic languages have no grammatical gender. In spoken Mandarin, the third-person pronoun tā is gender-neutral. Written Mandarin introduced gendered characters in the 20th century (他 masculine, 她 feminine, 它 non-human), but these are orthographic conventions, not grammatical gender — they are pronounced identically. Other Sinitic varieties generally do not have even this orthographic distinction.

linguisticChallenges.classifierSelection: Every noun requires a specific classifier (量词/measure word) when counted or used with demonstratives. Mandarin has 100+ classifiers; Cantonese has a similarly large set. Using the wrong classifier (e.g., *一个马 instead of 一匹马) is a clear non-native error. The general classifier 个/個 is overused by MT and signals poor quality.
linguisticChallenges.characterVariants: Written Chinese uses two standard character sets: Simplified Chinese (简体字, mainland China/Singapore) and Traditional Chinese (繁體字, Taiwan/Hong Kong/Macau). These are NOT interchangeable — using the wrong variant for the target region is unacceptable. Beyond Simplified/Traditional, there are variant characters (異體字) and region-specific preferences.
linguisticChallenges.topicProminence: Sinitic languages are fundamentally topic-prominent — the topic of a sentence is fronted and may have no grammatical role in the comment. English SVO translations must restructure topic-comment sentences, not just reorder words.
linguisticChallenges.proDrop: Subject and object pronouns are routinely dropped when recoverable from context. Over-generating pronouns (a common MT error from English-trained models) sounds extremely unnatural in Chinese.
linguisticChallenges.tonalDiacriticsInRomanization: When romanized output is needed (Pinyin for Mandarin, Jyutping for Cantonese), tone marks are essential for disambiguation. Omitting tone marks creates massive ambiguity — Mandarin has ~400 unique syllables but ~1,300+ with tone distinctions.
linguisticChallenges.measureWords: Beyond classifiers, Chinese uses specific measure words for uncountable quantities that differ from English conventions. Quantities that are countable in English may require measure words in Chinese, and vice versa.
linguisticChallenges.analyticGrammar: Sinitic languages are analytic/isolating — no inflection, no conjugation, no declension. Tense, aspect, and mood are expressed through particles (了, 着, 过, 会, 要) and adverbs, not verb forms. This means translation from inflected languages requires explicit particle insertion.

genus-sinitic.notes: Genus card for Sinitic (Chinese) languages (Mandarin, Cantonese/Yue, Wu/Shanghainese, Min, Hakka, Gan, Xiang, etc.). Script is 'Hani' (Han/CJK characters) — all varieties use Chinese characters as primary script. The macrolanguage-zho.json card provides specific properties for the Chinese macrolanguage grouping.

regions.region: China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, Singapore, Malaysia, global diaspora

genus-slavic.name: Slavic Languages

formality.description: All major Slavic languages have a T-V pronominal distinction: Russian ты/вы, Polish ty/pan/pani, Czech ty/vy, Serbian ti/vi, etc. Polish is particularly complex, using third-person pan/pani forms alongside second-person vy. Formality also interacts with verb forms and, in languages with case, the vocative case for address.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: All Slavic languages have a three-gender system: masculine, feminine, and neuter. Gender triggers agreement on adjectives, verbs (in past tense), pronouns, and numerals. Some Slavic languages further subdivide masculine into animate and inanimate (e.g., Polish, Czech, Russian in accusative). Gender assignment is partly morphological (word ending) and partly arbitrary.

linguisticChallenges.aspectualPairs: Slavic verbal aspect (perfective vs. imperfective) is the single most challenging feature for MT. Nearly every verb exists as an aspectual pair — the imperfective form denotes ongoing/habitual/repeated action, the perfective form denotes completed/bounded action. English does not grammaticalize this distinction the same way. Choosing the wrong aspect changes meaning fundamentally.
linguisticChallenges.complexCaseSystems: Most Slavic languages have 6–7 cases (nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, instrumental, locative, and vocative in some). Case endings interact with gender, number, and animacy. Nouns, adjectives, pronouns, and numerals all decline. Getting case wrong is the most visible translation error.
linguisticChallenges.motionVerbs: Slavic languages distinguish determinate (one-directional, in-progress) from indeterminate (habitual, multidirectional) motion verbs — e.g., Russian идти/ходить ('go on foot' determinate/indeterminate). Prefixed perfective motion verbs add further complexity. English 'go' maps to multiple distinct Slavic verbs.
linguisticChallenges.wordOrderFlexibility: While basic word order is SVO, Slavic languages have highly flexible pragmatic word order. Topic/focus structure determines word position — new information typically appears sentence-finally. Translation must respect information structure, not just syntactic slots.
linguisticChallenges.verbsOfMotion: The system of motion verbs with prefixes creates a vast network of spatial/aspectual meanings. Each directional prefix (в-, вы-, при-, у-, пере-, etc.) modifies both direction and aspect. This system has no equivalent in non-Slavic languages.
linguisticChallenges.numericAgreement: Slavic numeral agreement is notoriously complex. In Russian: 1 + nominative singular, 2–4 + genitive singular, 5–20 + genitive plural, 21 + nominative singular again. Polish and Czech have different but equally complex patterns. CLDR plural categories (one/few/many/other) capture this partially.

genus-slavic.notes: Genus card for Slavic languages (Russian, Ukrainian, Polish, Czech, Serbian, Croatian, Bulgarian, etc.). Script is null because the genus splits between Cyrillic (Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Macedonian) and Latin (Polish, Czech, Slovak, Croatian, Slovenian). Serbian uses both. All share the aspectual system, case system, and three-gender agreement.

regions.region: Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Balkans (Serbia, Croatia, Bulgaria, etc.), Belarus

macrolanguage-ara.name: Arabic Macrolanguage

formality.description: Arabic formality operates on two axes: MSA/dialect register choice and within-register politeness. MSA is inherently formal. Dialects have their own politeness systems using plural forms for singular formal address (inta/intu), honorific titles, and elaborate greeting protocols. All varieties share the cultural emphasis on respectful address through titles and kinship terms.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: All Arabic varieties have a pervasive masculine/feminine gender system affecting nouns, verbs, adjectives, pronouns, demonstratives, and numerals. Second-person pronouns distinguish gender of the addressee. Numerals 3–10 show reverse gender agreement (feminine numeral with masculine noun). Default to masculine for unknown referents in all varieties.

linguisticChallenges.diglossia: Arabic exhibits extreme diglossia — Modern Standard Arabic (MSA/fuṣḥā) is the written/formal standard across all regions, while daily communication uses mutually varying regional dialects (Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Maghreb, etc.). MT must determine target register: MSA for formal/written content, dialect for conversational content. Mixing registers sounds jarring.
linguisticChallenges.rootMorphology: All Arabic varieties share the triconsonantal root system. The root k-t-b yields: kataba 'wrote', kitāb 'book', kātib 'writer', maktaba 'library', iktitāb 'subscription'. Understanding root extraction is essential for morphological analysis and dictionary lookup.
linguisticChallenges.brokenPlurals: Arabic uses both 'sound' plurals (suffixed: -āt feminine, -ūn/-īn masculine) and 'broken' plurals (internal vowel changes: kitāb→kutub, walad→awlād). There are 30+ broken plural patterns. The choice between sound and broken plural is lexically determined and unpredictable.
linguisticChallenges.shortVowelOmission: Standard Arabic script omits short vowels (harakat/tashkeel). The word كتب can be read as kataba, kutiba, kutub, or kattaba. Context disambiguation is essential. Fully vowelized text is rare outside Quran, children's texts, and language learning materials.
linguisticChallenges.constructState: The iḍāfa (construct state) links nouns in genitive chains: bayt ar-rajul 'house of the man'. The first noun loses its definite article and final vowel. Chains can extend to 3+ nouns. This structure is used for possession, description, and compound nouns.
linguisticChallenges.dualNumber: Arabic preserves a productive dual number (singular/dual/plural) in nouns, verbs, pronouns, and adjectives. The dual form is mandatory for exactly two referents. Most target languages only have singular/plural and must paraphrase the dual.
linguisticChallenges.dialectalMorphology: Each major dialect region has its own morphological patterns, phonology, vocabulary, and syntax that differ substantially from MSA and from each other. Egyptian biyiktib vs. Levantine byuktob vs. Gulf yiktib for 'he writes'. Do NOT mix dialectal features.

macrolanguage-ara.notes: Macrolanguage card for Arabic (ara). Covers 28+ member varieties: Egyptian (arz), Levantine (apc/ajp), Gulf (afb), Moroccan (ary), Algerian (arq), Tunisian (aeb), Iraqi (acm), Sudanese (apd), Modern Standard Arabic (arb), and others. All share Arabic script, RTL direction, root-based morphology, M/F gender, and construct state. Diglossia between MSA and dialects is the central challenge.

regions.region: Middle East, North Africa (22 Arab League countries), plus diaspora communities worldwide

macrolanguage-fas.name: Persian Macrolanguage

formality.description: Persian has an exceptionally elaborate formality system (taarof/تعارف) that pervades all communication. Three or more pronoun levels exist: to (تو, intimate), shomā (شما, standard formal), and additional honorific forms. Formal register uses distinct vocabulary for common verbs: tashrif āvardan instead of āmadan for 'to come'. Self-deprecating and other-elevating conventions are deeply embedded. All Persian varieties share this system, though the specific vocabulary differs between Farsi, Dari, and Tajik.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Persian has no grammatical gender. The third-person pronoun u/ān (او/آن) is entirely gender-neutral. No agreement system is affected by gender. When translating from gendered source languages, gender must be expressed lexically if needed.

linguisticChallenges.ezafeConstruction: All Persian varieties use the ezāfe (اضافه) construction — a connecting particle (-e/-ye in Farsi/Dari, -i in Tajik) linking nouns to modifiers: ketāb-e bozorg 'big book' (lit. book-of big). Ezāfe chains extend to multiple modifiers and possessors. This is the fundamental modifier-linking mechanism and has no English equivalent.
linguisticChallenges.lightVerbSystem: Persian forms the vast majority of its predicates using light verb constructions: noun/adjective + light verb. There are only ~250 simple verbs in Persian, but thousands of compound verb expressions. kār kardan 'work do' = 'to work', dust dāshtan 'friend have' = 'to love'. These cannot be translated word-by-word.
linguisticChallenges.scriptVariation: While all standard Persian uses Arabic-derived script (RTL), the varieties differ: Farsi (Iran) and Dari (Afghanistan) use Perso-Arabic script with additional letters (پ چ ژ گ). Tajik historically used Perso-Arabic, then Latin, now primarily Cyrillic. Script-specific handling is needed per variety.
linguisticChallenges.differentialObjectMarking: The postposition -rā (را) marks specific/definite direct objects. Indefinite objects are unmarked: ketāb khāndam 'I read a book' vs. ketāb-rā khāndam 'I read the book'. This system has no exact English parallel.
linguisticChallenges.complexPredicates: Beyond light verbs, Persian uses preverbal elements that modify verb meaning extensively. Many expressions are idiomatic: dast-e kasi-rā gereftani 'to take someone's hand' = 'to help someone'. These must be translated as units.
linguisticChallenges.varietalDifferences: Farsi (Iran), Dari (Afghanistan), and Tajik (Tajikistan) share core grammar but differ in vocabulary, pronunciation, some syntax, and script. Dari retains some features lost in Farsi. Tajik has absorbed Russian vocabulary. Do NOT interchange variety-specific vocabulary.

macrolanguage-fas.notes: Macrolanguage card for Persian (fas). Covers Western Farsi (pes, Iran), Dari (prs, Afghanistan), and Tajik (tgk, Tajikistan). All share SOV order, ezāfe construction, light verb system, no grammatical gender, and the taarof formality system. Script is Arabic-derived for Farsi/Dari (RTL), but Tajik uses Cyrillic (LTR) — the primary script 'Arab' reflects the majority.

regions.region: Iran (Farsi), Afghanistan (Dari), Tajikistan (Tajik)

macrolanguage-kur.name: Kurdish Macrolanguage

formality.description: Kurdish varieties have T-V pronominal distinctions: Kurmanji tu/hûn, Sorani to/êwe. Formal address uses plural pronouns for singular referents. Formality is also expressed through vocabulary choice and discourse particles. The system is similar across varieties despite script and structural differences.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Gender varies WITHIN the macrolanguage: Kurmanji (Northern Kurdish) retains a full masculine/feminine gender system with agreement on articles, adjectives, and verbs. Sorani (Central Kurdish) has LOST grammatical gender — no gender agreement, gender-neutral pronouns. This is a fundamental structural difference between the two main varieties. Cards for individual varieties MUST override this field.

linguisticChallenges.scriptSplit: Kurdish varieties use different scripts: Kurmanji (Northern Kurdish) uses Latin script (Hawar alphabet, LTR) in Turkey and Syria. Sorani (Central Kurdish) uses modified Arabic/Persian script (RTL) in Iraq and Iran. This is NOT just a transliteration difference — orthographic conventions, word boundaries, and even morphological representation differ by script. MT must handle both scripts correctly.
linguisticChallenges.splitErgativity: Both major Kurdish varieties exhibit split ergativity — ergative-absolutive alignment in past tenses (the agent of a past transitive verb takes oblique case) and nominative-accusative in present tenses. The ergative split is more prominent in Kurmanji than Sorani.
linguisticChallenges.ezafeConstruction: Both varieties use the ezāfe construction (Kurmanji -a/-ê/-ên, Sorani -î/-y) to link nouns to modifiers, shared with Persian. Ezāfe forms differ by variety and interact with gender (in Kurmanji) and definiteness.
linguisticChallenges.genderAsymmetry: Kurmanji's full M/F gender system vs. Sorani's genderless system is the most dramatic structural difference within a single macrolanguage. MT systems must apply completely different agreement rules depending on the target variety.
linguisticChallenges.lightVerbs: Both varieties use light verb constructions shared with the Iranian genus: noun/adjective + light verb (kirin 'to do', bûn 'to become', dan 'to give', etc.). Compound verb inventories differ between Kurmanji and Sorani.
linguisticChallenges.dialectContinuum: Kurdish forms a dialect continuum — Kurmanji, Sorani, and Southern Kurdish (Kelhuri/Feyli) grade into each other geographically.
