Written standards exist for Kurmanji and Sorani but are not fully standardized. Vocabulary, morphology, and syntax all show continuous variation.

macrolanguage-kur.notes: Macrolanguage card for Kurdish (kur). Covers Kurmanji/Northern Kurdish (kmr, Latin script), Sorani/Central Kurdish (ckb, Arabic script), and Southern Kurdish (sdh). Script and direction are null because of the Latin (LTR)/Arabic (RTL) split. Gender is null because Kurmanji has it and Sorani doesn't. Individual variety cards MUST override script, dir, and gender.

regions.region: Turkey (Kurmanji), Iraq (Sorani, official in Kurdistan Region), Iran (Sorani/Southern), Syria (Kurmanji)

macrolanguage-lah.name: Lahnda (Western Panjabi) Macrolanguage

formality.description: Lahnda varieties share the Indic multi-level honorific system inherited from the genus. Multiple pronoun levels distinguish intimate, familiar, and respectful address. Verb conjugation changes with each level. Western Panjabi varieties additionally encode religious and community identity through formality choices (Islamic honorifics, Sikh honorifics).

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Lahnda varieties have a binary masculine/feminine gender system inherited from Indo-Aryan. Gender triggers agreement on verbs, adjectives, and postpositions. Gender assignment is partly morphological (word ending) and partly arbitrary.

linguisticChallenges.scriptDiversity: Lahnda varieties use multiple scripts: Shahmukhi (modified Arabic/Perso-Arabic script, RTL) is used by Muslim communities in Pakistan. Gurmukhi (Indic script, LTR) is used by Sikh communities. Latin (LTR) is used informally, especially in digital communication. The Shahmukhi/Gurmukhi split makes script and direction null at the macrolanguage level.
linguisticChallenges.tonalVariation: Some Lahnda varieties (including Saraiki and some Western Panjabi dialects) have developed lexical tone from the loss of aspiration and voicing contrasts. Tonal systems are not uniform across the macrolanguage — some varieties are tonal, others are not.
linguisticChallenges.postpositionalSystem: All varieties are strictly SOV with postpositions, shared with the broader Indic genus. Case relations are expressed through postpositions that follow the noun.
linguisticChallenges.compoundVerbs: Light verb and conjunct verb constructions are pervasive, inherited from the Indic genus. Predicates are formed by combining nouns/adjectives with light verbs (karnā, honā, etc.).
linguisticChallenges.dialectContinuum: Lahnda varieties form a dialect continuum with Eastern Panjabi (pan) and Sindhi. Boundaries between 'Lahnda varieties' and neighboring languages are linguistically gradient rather than sharp. The macrolanguage grouping is partly administrative.
linguisticChallenges.lowResourceStatus: Most Lahnda varieties have very limited digital presence and NLP resources. MT quality for these varieties is expected to be significantly lower than for major world languages. Community-validated resources are scarce.

macrolanguage-lah.notes: Macrolanguage card for Lahnda/Western Panjabi (lah). Covers Western Panjabi (pnb), Saraiki (skr), Hindko (hnd/hno), Pahari-Potwari (phr), and other varieties. Script and direction are null because of the Shahmukhi (RTL)/Gurmukhi (LTR) split. Individual variety cards must specify script and direction.

regions.region: Pakistan (Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh border), India (Jammu)

macrolanguage-msa.name: Malay Macrolanguage

formality.description: Malay varieties express formality through pronoun choice (aku/saya informal/formal in Malaysian, aku/saya in Indonesian), vocabulary register (colloquial vs. standard), and discourse particles. Indonesian and Malaysian Malay share the aku/saya distinction but have divergent formal vocabulary. Honorific titles (Tuan, Puan, Encik, Bapak/Ibu) are widely used.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Malay varieties have no grammatical gender. Pronouns are gender-neutral (dia 'he/she'). Gender is expressed lexically when needed (lelaki 'male', perempuan 'female'). No agreement system is affected by gender.

linguisticChallenges.affixationSystem: Malay has a productive affixation system using prefixes (meN-, peN-, ber-, di-, ter-), suffixes (-kan, -i, -an), and circumfixes (meN-...-kan, peN-...-an, ke-...-an). These affixes derive nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs from roots. The nasal prefix meN- undergoes complex assimilation: menulis (tulis→menulis), membaca (baca→membaca), menyapu (sapu→menyapu). MT frequently produces incorrect affix forms.
linguisticChallenges.reduplication: Full and partial reduplication is highly productive: rumah→rumah-rumah 'houses', sayur-mayur 'various vegetables', lauk-pauk 'various dishes'. Reduplication expresses plurality, variety, intensity, and approximation. MT systems often fail to generate or interpret reduplicated forms.
linguisticChallenges.regionalDivergence: Malaysian Malay (Bahasa Melayu) and Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia) have diverged significantly in vocabulary, spelling conventions, and some grammar despite shared roots. saya (ID: formal 'I') vs. saya (MY: standard 'I'); kereta (MY: 'car') vs. mobil (ID: 'car'); pejabat (MY: 'office') vs. kantor (ID: 'office'). Never mix Malaysian and Indonesian vocabulary.
linguisticChallenges.activePassiveVoice: Malay has a prominent passive voice using the prefix di- that is used far more frequently than English passive. Active meN- and passive di- form a core voice alternation. There is also an informal passive using the bare root with a fronted agent.
linguisticChallenges.noInflection: Malay is an analytic language with no verb conjugation, no noun declension, and no grammatical agreement of any kind. Tense is expressed through temporal adverbs (sudah 'already', akan 'will', sedang 'currently') or context. This can lead to ambiguity when translating from tense-marked source languages.
linguisticChallenges.classificationNote: Malay is Austronesian (Malayo-Polynesian), but this macrolanguage card sets extends: null to avoid dependency on a genus card that does not yet exist. Future update should set extends to the appropriate Malayo-Polynesian genus when created.

macrolanguage-msa.notes: Macrolanguage card for Malay (msa). Covers Indonesian (ind), Malaysian Malay (zsm), and other varieties. All share Latin script, SVO order, agglutinative affixation, reduplication, and lack of grammatical gender. Extends is null because the appropriate Malayo-Polynesian genus card does not yet exist — should be updated when one is created.

regions.region: Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, East Timor

macrolanguage-nor.name: Norwegian Macrolanguage

formality.description: Norwegian historically had a T-V distinction (du/De), but De has become almost completely archaic in modern use. Contemporary Norwegian uses universal du for all contexts, similar to the Swedish du-reform. The formal De may appear in very traditional or ceremonial contexts. Formality is now primarily expressed through vocabulary choice and discourse style rather than pronoun selection.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Both Norwegian written standards have grammatical gender. Bokmål has three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) though feminine is optional — two-gender (common/neuter) usage is also accepted. Nynorsk strictly maintains three genders. Gender triggers agreement on articles, adjectives, and pronouns. The optional feminine in Bokmål creates a sociolinguistic choice (using feminine is perceived as less conservative).

linguisticChallenges.twoWrittenStandards: Norwegian has two official written standards: Bokmål (used by ~85–90% of the population, historically influenced by Danish) and Nynorsk (used by ~10–15%, based on Norwegian dialects). They share grammar but differ in vocabulary, morphology, and spelling. MT output MUST use the correct standard for the target audience — mixing standards is unacceptable.
linguisticChallenges.v2WordOrder: Norwegian follows V2 word order in main clauses — the finite verb must be the second constituent. Subordinate clauses have different word order (SVO with adverb placement before the verb). This alternation must be maintained.
linguisticChallenges.compoundWords: Norwegian forms compound nouns by concatenation without spaces: samferdseldepartementet ('transportation department'). Compound splitting and formation are both error-prone. Incorrect spacing (samferdsel departementet) is a visible error.
linguisticChallenges.suffixedDefiniteArticle: Norwegian suffixes the definite article to the noun: hus→huset ('the house'), bok→boka/boken ('the book'). With adjectives, both a freestanding article AND the suffixed article are used (double definiteness): det store huset ('the big house'). This interaction is a consistent MT error source.
linguisticChallenges.bokmaalNynorskDifferences: Key systematic differences: Bokmål -ene/-ene plurals vs. Nynorsk -ane/-ene; Bokmål optional feminine vs. Nynorsk mandatory feminine; Bokmål passive -s vs. Nynorsk bli + past participle; Bokmål loanword spelling closer to Danish vs. Nynorsk native-based forms.
linguisticChallenges.dialectalVariation: Norwegian has extreme dialectal variation — spoken Norwegian differs dramatically by region. Written standards do not directly correspond to any spoken dialect. Dialectal forms sometimes appear in informal writing and must not be mixed with standard forms.

macrolanguage-nor.notes: Macrolanguage card for Norwegian (nor). Covers Bokmål (nob) and Nynorsk (nno). Both share Latin script, V2 word order, three-gender system, and suffixed definite articles. The two-standard situation is the central challenge — MT must produce output in the correct standard.

regions.region: Norway (Bokmål dominant in cities/east, Nynorsk in western/rural areas)

macrolanguage-sqi.name: Albanian Macrolanguage

formality.description: Albanian has a T-V distinction: ti (singular informal) vs. ju (plural/formal). Formal address uses second-person plural verb forms with singular reference. Honorific titles (Zotëri, Zonja) are used in formal contexts. The T-V system is actively used in all Albanian-speaking regions.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Albanian has a three-gender system: masculine, feminine, and neuter (neuter merges with masculine in plural). Gender triggers agreement on articles, adjectives, and pronouns. Albanian uses both preposed and postposed (suffixed) definite articles, with the suffixed article being the primary form.

linguisticChallenges.suffixedDefiniteArticle: Albanian suffixes the definite article to the noun: libër→libri 'the book', shtëpi→shtëpia 'the house'. The suffix varies by gender, number, and case. This is a Balkan sprachbund feature shared with Romanian and Bulgarian but not with most other Indo-European languages.
linguisticChallenges.balkanSprachbund: Albanian shares structural features with unrelated Balkan languages (Romanian, Bulgarian, Greek) due to centuries of contact: postposed definite article, loss of infinitive (replaced by subjunctive constructions with të), clitic doubling, and merged dative-genitive case.
linguisticChallenges.caseSystem: Albanian has five cases (nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, ablative) with distinct definite and indefinite declension paradigms. Adjectives also decline for case, gender, and definiteness.
linguisticChallenges.ghegToskDifferences: The two main Albanian varieties — Gheg (northern, spoken in Kosovo, northern Albania, North Macedonia) and Tosk (southern, basis of standard Albanian in Albania) — differ in phonology (Gheg has nasal vowels), some morphology (Gheg preserves infinitive), and vocabulary. Standard Albanian is based primarily on Tosk.
linguisticChallenges.admirativeAndEvidentiality: Albanian has a grammaticalized admirative mood (mënyra habitore) that expresses surprise, reported information, or non-firsthand evidence. This evidential/mirative category has no grammatical equivalent in most target languages and must be paraphrased.

macrolanguage-sqi.notes: Macrolanguage card for Albanian (sqi). Covers Tosk Albanian (als, southern/standard) and Gheg Albanian (aln, northern/Kosovo). Both share Latin script, SVO order, M/F/N gender, suffixed definite articles, and Balkan sprachbund features. Albanian forms its own branch of Indo-European with no close relatives.

regions.region: Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia (western), Montenegro, southern Serbia, diaspora in Greece/Italy

macrolanguage-swa.name: Swahili Macrolanguage

formality.description: Swahili expresses formality through pronoun choice (wewe/ninyi for singular familiar/plural-as-formal), honorific titles (Bwana, Bibi, Mzee), and vocabulary register. Formal Swahili draws on Arabic-origin vocabulary and standard Kiswahili sanifu. Informal registers use more local dialect features and English/local language borrowings.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Swahili uses a noun class system (18 classes, typically grouped into 9 singular/plural pairs) rather than grammatical gender. Noun classes categorize by semantic and morphological properties (human, non-human animate, plants, abstracts, augmentative, diminutive, locative, etc.). The human class (M/WA) is the closest to 'gender' but distinguishes human/non-human, not masculine/feminine.

linguisticChallenges.nounClassAgreement: Swahili noun classes trigger agreement chains across entire sentences. Subject prefix, object infix, adjective prefix, demonstrative, possessive, and relative marker all agree with the noun class: ki-tabu ki-zuri ki-le ki-moja 'that one beautiful book' (all ki- class 7). Getting class agreement wrong is immediately noticeable.
linguisticChallenges.agglutinativeVerbMorphology: Swahili verbs carry subject prefix + tense marker + (object infix) + root + (derivational suffixes) + final vowel: a-na-ki-soma 'he/she-PRESENT-it(cl7)-reads'. A single verb form can be 5–7 morphemes long. Morpheme boundary errors are common in MT.
linguisticChallenges.arabicVocabularyInfluence: Swahili has extensive Arabic borrowings (estimated 20–40% of core vocabulary) from centuries of Indian Ocean trade. These loanwords are fully integrated into Swahili noun class and morphology systems. Some Arabic plurals coexist with Swahili class plurals for the same noun.
linguisticChallenges.standardVsDialect: Standard Swahili (Kiswahili sanifu) is based on the Zanzibar/Unguja dialect but differs from other Swahili varieties (Congo Swahili, Kimvita/Mombasa, Kiamu, etc.). Congo Swahili in particular has simplified noun class agreement. Do NOT mix dialect features with standard Swahili.
linguisticChallenges.tenseAspectSystem: Swahili has a rich tense/aspect system expressed through verbal prefixes: -na- (present/progressive), -li- (past), -ta- (future), -me- (perfect/completive), -ki- (conditional/temporal), -nge- (hypothetical), -ngali- (counterfactual). These are not simple equivalents to English tenses.
linguisticChallenges.derivationalSuffixes: Productive derivational suffixes modify verb meaning: -isha (causative), -iwa (passive), -ana (reciprocal), -ia (applicative), -ika (stative). These can stack: pend-esh-an-a 'love-CAUS-RECIP-FV' = 'cause each other to love'. MT must handle these combinations.

contactInfluences.notes: Centuries of Indian Ocean trade brought extensive Arabic vocabulary. Swahili was historically written in Arabic script (Ajami). Arabic influence is strongest in coastal dialects and formal register.
British colonial influence in East Africa. English loanwords dominate technology, education, and modern commerce domains.

macrolanguage-swa.notes: Macrolanguage card for Swahili (swa). Covers Swahili proper (swh, Tanzania/Kenya) and Congo Swahili (swc, DRC). Both share Latin script, SVO word order, noun class system, and agglutinative Bantu morphology. Arabic vocabulary influence is a distinctive shared feature.

regions.region: Tanzania (national), Kenya (official), DRC (national), Uganda, Comoros, Mozambique

macrolanguage-zho.name: Chinese Macrolanguage

formality.description: Chinese varieties share a register-based formality system expressed through vocabulary choice (colloquial vs. literary), discourse particles, and specific honorific/humble word pairs. Mandarin has the nǐ/nín (你/您) T-V pronoun distinction. Written formal Chinese across all varieties draws on Classical Chinese (文言文) vocabulary. Cantonese, Wu, and other varieties rely more on lexical register than pronominal formality.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Chinese has no grammatical gender. The spoken third-person pronoun tā is gender-neutral across all varieties. Written Mandarin introduced gendered characters (他/她/它) in the 20th century as an orthographic convention — they share pronunciation. Other varieties generally do not distinguish gender in writing either.

linguisticChallenges.classifierSystem: All Chinese varieties use classifier/measure word systems. Each noun requires a specific classifier when counted or used with demonstratives. Classifier inventories and preferences differ between varieties (Mandarin vs. Cantonese classifiers are partially overlapping but not identical).
linguisticChallenges.simplifiedTraditional: The Chinese macrolanguage spans two standard character sets: Simplified (简体, mainland China/Singapore) and Traditional (繁體, Taiwan/Hong Kong/Macau). Output MUST use the correct variant for the target region. One-to-many and many-to-one character mappings exist between the sets — conversion is not trivial.
linguisticChallenges.tonalVariation: Tonal systems differ dramatically across varieties: Mandarin has 4 tones (+neutral), Cantonese 6–9, Min varieties 7–8, Wu 5–7. Romanization systems differ accordingly (Pinyin, Jyutping, POJ). Tone marks are essential for disambiguation in all romanized output.
linguisticChallenges.topicDrop: All Chinese varieties are strongly topic-prominent and pro-drop. Subjects, objects, and topics are omitted when recoverable. Over-generating pronouns is the most common MT error in Chinese output.
linguisticChallenges.analyticGrammar: No inflection across any variety. Tense/aspect/mood expressed through particles that differ between varieties (Mandarin 了/着/过 vs. Cantonese 咗/緊/過). Particle systems are NOT interchangeable between varieties.
linguisticChallenges.mutualIntelligibility: Chinese varieties are NOT mutually intelligible in spoken form — Mandarin, Cantonese, Wu, Min, Hakka are as different as Romance languages. However, they share a written standard (with variation). Do NOT treat Chinese as a single spoken language.

macrolanguage-zho.notes: Macrolanguage card for Chinese (zho). Covers 15+ member varieties (Mandarin cmn, Cantonese yue, Wu wuu, Min Nan nan, Min Dong cdo, Hakka hak, Gan gan, Xiang hsn, etc.). All share CJK characters, analytic grammar, classifier systems, and topic-prominence. Individual variety cards should extend this card.

regions.region: China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, Singapore, Malaysia, global diaspora

Spoken in the Northwest Territories between Great Slave Lake and Great Bear Lake. It is the first language of 2,470 people (of whom about 1,350 regularly use it in the home), primarily in five small communities: Detah (105 speakers out of a total population of 190), Rae Lakes (210 out of 260), Rae-Edzo (1,010 out of 1,655), Snare
Lake (100 out of 135), and Wha Ti (325 out of 415). There are also about 220 speakers in the city of Yellowknife, as well as an unknown number of speakers in the dialectally mixed community of Déline (Fort Franklin).

Widely used throughout southeastern Ghana and southern Togo, it is believed that the Éwé migrated south from Nigeria in the 13th century into the Tado region of present-day Togo. In the 18th century, they came in contact with Europeans and were involved in slave trade. Éwé is an official language in both Ghana and Togo. Éwé culture and tradition is rich in folklore, poetry, myths, and songs. Éwé is used in cultural activities, in commerce, weaving, education, farming, and fishing.

Preschools are mainly in Dutch, but Frisian is allowed as well. Some 20% of the preschools are joined in the SFBO, the Association of Frisian-language Childcare. These preschools are usually bilingual Dutch and Frisian.

In primary education Frisian has been a mandatory subject in all school years since 1980. Attainment targets for proficiency, vocabulary and language attitude have been prescribed by the government. However, inspections have shown that primary schools generally do not meet these targets, even after they were lowered in 2006. Official regulations do not specify how much time per week ought to be dedicated to Frisian. On average, primary schools spend some 40 minutes a week on Frisian, either by using the provincially sponsored learning method, using own materials, or by watching Frisian television. 55% of all primary school teachers are qualified to teach Frisian and in 40% of the primary schools Frisian is taught by unqualified teachers.

The position of Frisian is much stronger in trilingual primary schools, where Frisian, Dutch and English are languages of instructions. Typically, Frisian has a share of 50% of the curriculum in the first six years and 40% in the years 7 and 8 (next to 50% Dutch, and 40% Dutch and 20% English respectively). Of all primary schools in the province 17% are either certified as trilingual schools or in the process of attaining the certification. Unlike normal primary schools, trilingual schools to tend to meet the attainment targets set by the government.

According to law, Frisian is compulsory as a subject in the first half of secondary education. However, in practice, it is generally confined to a single hour in the first year. Frisian ought to be an optional subject in the second half of secondary education, but only some schools in fact offer this possibility. The number of pupils doing an exam in Frisian at the end of secondary school has risen from 46 pupils in 2011 to 85 pupils in 2015. In addition, there are three trilingual secondary schools, in which Frisian is language of instruction in at least one group for at least subject.

At the university level a Frisian programme is offered within the bachelor programme of Minorities and Multilingualism at the Rijksuniversiteit Groningen. The programme teaches Frisian writing proficiency as well as Frisian linguistics, literature, cultural history and Old Frisian. The University of Amsterdam offers a smaller programme (minor) in Frisian language. A teaching education programme for Frisian is provided for as an optional trajectory at the Stenden University for Applied Sciences in Leeuwarden.

The AFUK provides adult education in Frisian language for native speakers and beginners at different levels. [Endangerment.Certainty: 0.2]

It can be stated that the Frisian language is mainly spoken in the homes of Frisian people, in the countryside and in informal situations. In more formal surroundings, such as shops in town and government offices, many people shift to Dutch even if Frisian is their first language. In larger groups of people the presence of one Dutch speaking-person may suffice to trigger language shift of the whole group from Frisian to Dutch. Because of the fact that most Frisians (in particular the older ones) got their school education only in Dutch, many of them are not able to use the Frisian language in writing and prefer reading in Dutch... The provincial government of Friesland and a number of municipalities make frequent use of both written and spoken Frisian. The regional broadcasting company Omrop Fryslân does radio and television broadcasts. [Endangerment.Certainty: 0.4]

The University of Amsterdam offers a smaller programme (minor) in Frisian language. The province of Friesland has about 600,000 inhabitants and about half of these can be considered first-language speakers of Frisian. Speakers of Frisian form a (great) majority in most rural areas, and a (small) minority in the towns and citites, on the Frisian Isles and in the Stellingwerven (two Low-Saxon municipalities in the southeastern part of the province). speakerEstimates.note: According to the 1991 population census, Kaokoland is a district with an area of 58.190 km2 inhabited by a population of 26.313 people that is 1,88% of the total population of Namibia. Kaokoland is a multilingual district, where Otjiherero, Oshiwambo, Oluzimba, Olunkambwe, Otjingumbi, Otjitwa, Otjihakaona and Otjikuvare are spoken. Otjiherero is spoken by approximately 24.500 people that is 93,1% of the total population in Kaokoland. [Date Of Info: 1991]

The 1991 census counted some 113 000 speakers of Otjiherero, which constitutes approximately eight percent of the total population of Namibia... The entire Ovaherero population can be subdivided into four main groups, namely, the central Ovaherero in central Namibia, the Kaokolanders (or western Ovaherero) in Kaokoland, the Ovambanderu (or eastern Ovaherero) in eastern Namibia and the Botswana Ovaherero. The dialect spoken by the central Ovaherero is called Central Otjiherero, or just Otjiherero as it is the basis for standardisation (that is, the norm variety). The dialect spoken by the Ovambanderu, Otjimbanderu, is assumed to have been more divergent from Central Otjiherero in the past. Partly owing to the influence of the standardisation of Central Otjiherero, the two dialects have largely converged, or rather, the distinctiveness of Otjimbanderu has suffered under the influence of the standardised Central Otjiherero... In Kaokoland there are also several Angolan immigrant groups, many of which are either Ovaherero or at least closely related to the Ovaherero, andJ they speak mutually intelligible languages or even Otjiherero dialects, including Otjitwa, Otjihakaona, Otjikuvare, Oluthimba, Olungambwe, and Otjingumbi.

Segundo a lingüista Alzerinda de O. Braga, o português é hoje a língua de comunicação cotidiana entre a população jovem. Dos 75 Makurap que viviam no PI Guaporé no final da década de 1990, 45 ainda falavam a língua Makurap. Esta também é falada por muitos membros mais velhos dos outros grupos indígenas da região. Nas “chichadas” (festas com consumo coletivo de bebida fermentada de milho), os velhos dançam, brincam e falam em macurap independente de seu grupo étnico.

Nishnaabemwin (Eastern Ojibwe and Ottawa/Odawa): Nishnaabemwin represents the linguistic and social fusion of two historically distinct communities, the Ottawa (Odawa) and the Eastern Ojibwe. The homeland of the Ottawa dialect is on the north shores of Lake Huron, and the most vigorous community of speakers is at the Wikwemikong Reserve on Manitoulin Island, Ontario; there are also several hundred speakers in Michigan, with the largest community at the Isabella Reservation.  A number of Ottawas were relocated in Oklahoma during the 19th century, but the language does not survive there.  The principal Eastern Ojibwe communities are at Walpole Island on the Detroit River, on Parry Island, and at Curve Lake, near Peterborough.  In both Ontario and in Michigan there is considerable dialect mixture between Nishnaabemwin and Southwestern Ojibwe (here usually called “Chippewa”) and the distinction is sometimes hard to make.  The most clearly defined (and most vigorously surviving) variety is the Odawa of Manitoulin Island, where perhaps half of the population of over 3,000 has some fluency in the language.

25,900 (1998 Statistics Canada). Canada Census (2001) lists all Ojibwa varieties together as 30,505 population.

who are exposed to Pite Saami on a regular basis at all (pg. 302). and those who perhaps would want to be more active but have other commitments.
